json.stance: The rider asks for a partial refund of the excess distance fare because the driver deviated 4.3 km from the recommended route without notifying the rider.
json.requested_outcome: partial refund of the excess distance fare
json.brief: The platform record shows the trip ran 24.8 km against a recommended 20.5 km, a deviation of 4.3 km [E-TRP-01] [E-RTE-01]. GPS pings confirm the car left the PIE corridor and traveled through Geylang and onto the ECP [E-GPS-07] [E-GPS-08] [E-GPS-11]. This is well above the 1 km tolerance in [Section 1.3]. Under [Section 1.2] the driver must inform the rider of a deviation before or at the point of deviation, and the engine found no notice [FC-F05]. The chat has no route-change message from the driver. When the rider asked at 13:24 whether the route was right, the driver replied only "Don't worry, I know the way" and gave no reason [E-CHT-05] [E-CHT-06]. That reply is not a notice of a deviation and does not show the rider agreed [Section 1.4]. The matrix row for a traffic reroute with no notice and more than 1 km gives a partial refund of the excess distance fare [Section 1.3], consistent with [Precedent 7.1]. The excess distance fare is $3.44 [E-PAY-01]. The rider asks for that amount and leaves it to the Judge whether the $2.22 in excess tolls also belongs in the refund [E-PAY-01].

arguments.point: The deviation was 4.3 km, far above the 1 km tolerance, and GPS confirms the route departed from the recommended PIE path.
The driver gave no notice of the reroute. The only reply to the rider's question about the route offered no reason and no mention of a change, so there was no notice and no agreement.

The matrix row for an unnotified reroute over 1 km gives a partial refund of the excess distance fare, and Precedent 7.1 applied the same remedy where traffic justified the reroute but the rider was not told.
The rider raised the concern mid-trip and was brushed off, which shows the lack of notice was not the rider's oversight.

weaknesses.point: The driver will say the reroute was justified: a PIE vehicle fire and airport exit congestion were recorded, and the ECP was flowing smoothly. The engine found the traffic justification established, so the rider is not entitled to a full refund, only a partial one.
The rider's ticket says the trip took 37 minutes against 35 estimated and that the usual fare is about $28. The trip was only 2 minutes longer, and the ticket is the rider's own statement.

The refund is limited to the excess distance fare of $3.44, less than the $6.50 total difference the rider claims. The $2.22 in excess tolls is separate from the distance fare and may not be refundable under the matrix.

The ECP was flowing smoothly, and the record describes the driver's ECP reroute as a reasonable alternative [E-TRF-03]. The GPS shows steady progress, with speeds of 70 to 75 km/h on the ECP and no speed anomalies [E-GPS-11] [E-GPS-12]. The trip took 37 minutes against 35 estimated, so the rider lost almost no time [E-TRP-01]. That is the outcome Section 1.1 permits, because drivers may reroute for congestion [Section 1.1]. Because the reroute was justified, the full-refund row for an unjustified reroute does not apply [Section 1.3]. The correct row is the partial refund of the excess distance fare, as in [Precedent 7.1]. That precedent's refund was limited to the excess distance fare, not the whole trip [Precedent 7.1]. Here that fare is $3.44 [E-PAY-01]. The $2.22 in tolls is a separate line, and the matrix refers only to the excess distance fare [E-PAY-01] [Section 1.3].

arguments.point: The reroute was justified by verified traffic: a PIE vehicle fire and airport-exit congestion were recorded while the ECP was clear. The full-refund row therefore does not apply.
The remedy under the matrix and Precedent 7.1 is limited to the excess distance fare of $3.44. Tolls are not part of that remedy, and the rider's $6.50 claim overstates it.
The rider suffered no real time loss. The trip ran 37 minutes against 35 estimated, and the ECP was moving at speed, which supports the reasonableness of the reroute.

The driver did respond when the rider asked about the route, and reassured the rider that the trip would arrive on time. The trip did arrive within the estimated time, which shows the reassurance was borne out.

rebuttals.reply: The deviation is not disputed, but a deviation above 1 km only triggers the matrix. It does not show wrongdoing, because the reroute was justified by traffic.
The driver gave no express notice, which the driver concedes. That fact only moves the case to the partial-refund row. It does not support a larger remedy.

The driver agrees the partial-refund row applies. Both the matrix and Precedent 7.1 limit the refund to the excess distance fare of $3.44, and neither mentions tolls, so the $2.22 in tolls should not be added.

The chat shows the rider asked about the route and got a brief reply. That is a courtesy point and does not change the matrix outcome. The rider also did not ask to change course, and the trip arrived on schedule.

concessions.point: The route was 4.3 km longer than recommended, which is well above the 1 km tolerance.

json.brief: The platform record shows the trip ran 24.8 km against a recommended 20.5 km, a deviation of 4.3 km [E-TRP-01] [E-RTE-01]. GPS pings confirm the car left the PIE corridor and traveled through Geylang and onto the ECP [E-GPS-07] [E-GPS-08] [E-GPS-11]. This is well above the 1 km tolerance in [Section 1.3]. Under [Section 1.2] the driver must inform the rider of a deviation before or at the point of deviation, and the engine found no notice [FC-F05]. The chat has no route-change message from the driver. When the rider asked at 13:24 whether the route was right, the driver replied only "Don't worry, I know the way" and gave no reason [E-CHT-05] [E-CHT-06]. That reply is not a notice of a deviation and does not show the rider agreed [Section 1.4]. The matrix row for a traffic reroute with no notice and more than 1 km gives a partial refund of the excess distance fare [Section 1.3], consistent with [Precedent 7.1]. The excess distance fare is $3.44 [E-PAY-01]. The rider asks for that amount and leaves it to the Judge whether the $2.22 in excess tolls also belongs in the refund [E-PAY-01].

arguments.point: The deviation was 4.3 km, far above the 1 km tolerance, and GPS confirms the route departed from the recommended PIE path.
The driver gave no notice of the reroute. The only reply to the rider's question about the route offered no reason and no mention of a change, so there was no notice and no agreement.

The matrix row for an unnotified reroute over 1 km gives a partial refund of the excess distance fare, and Precedent 7.1 applied the same remedy where traffic justified the reroute but the rider was not told.
The rider raised the concern mid-trip and was brushed off, which shows the lack of notice was not the rider's oversight.

weaknesses.point: The driver will say the reroute was justified: a PIE vehicle fire and airport exit congestion were recorded, and the ECP was flowing smoothly. The engine found the traffic justification established, so the rider is not entitled to a full refund, only a partial one.
The rider's ticket says the trip took 37 minutes against 35 estimated and that the usual fare is about $28. The trip was only 2 minutes longer, and the ticket is the rider's own statement.

The refund is limited to the excess distance fare of $3.44, less than the $6.50 total difference the rider claims. The $2.22 in excess tolls is separate from the distance fare and may not be refundable under the matrix.

json.brief: The engine established that the reroute was justified by traffic [E-TRF-01] [E-TRF-02]. A vehicle fire blocked lanes 1 and 2 on the PIE eastbound from 13:05 until 13:50, with secondary congestion at the airport exit from 13:15 to 13:40 [E-TRF-01] [E-TRF-02]. The ECP was flowing smoothly, and the record describes the driver's ECP reroute as a reasonable alternative [E-TRF-03]. The GPS shows steady progress, with speeds of 70 to 75 km/h on the ECP and no speed anomalies [E-GPS-11] [E-GPS-12]. The trip took 37 minutes against 35 estimated, so the rider lost almost no time [E-TRP-01]. That is the outcome Section 1.1 permits, because drivers may reroute for congestion [Section 1.1]. Because the reroute was justified, the full-refund row for an unjustified reroute does not apply [Section 1.3]. The correct row is the partial refund of the excess distance fare, as in [Precedent 7.1]. That precedent's refund was limited to the excess distance fare, not the whole trip [Precedent 7.1]. Here that fare is $3.44 [E-PAY-01]. The $2.22 in tolls is a separate line, and the matrix refers only to the excess distance fare [E-PAY-01] [Section 1.3].

arguments.point: The reroute was justified by verified traffic: a PIE vehicle fire and airport-exit congestion were recorded while the ECP was clear. The full-refund row therefore does not apply.
The remedy under the matrix and Precedent 7.1 is limited to the excess distance fare of $3.44. Tolls are not part of that remedy, and the rider's $6.50 claim overstates it.
The rider suffered no real time loss. The trip ran 37 minutes against 35 estimated, and the ECP was moving at speed, which supports the reasonableness of the reroute.

The driver did respond when the rider asked about the route, and reassured the rider that the trip would arrive on time. The trip did arrive within the estimated time, which shows the reassurance was borne out.

rebuttals.reply: The deviation is not disputed, but a deviation above 1 km only triggers the matrix. It does not show wrongdoing, because the reroute was justified by traffic.
The driver gave no express notice, which the driver concedes. That fact only moves the case to the partial-refund row. It does not support a larger remedy.

The driver agrees the partial-refund row applies. Both the matrix and Precedent 7.1 limit the refund to the excess distance fare of $3.44, and neither mentions tolls, so the $2.22 in tolls should not be added.

The chat shows the rider asked about the route and got a brief reply. That is a courtesy point and does not change the matrix outcome. The rider also did not ask to change course, and the trip arrived on schedule.

concessions.point: The route was 4.3 km longer than recommended, which is well above the 1 km tolerance.
The driver did not inform the rider of the reroute. The only reply to the rider's route question gave no reason and no mention of a change, and no agreement is shown.
